chunks: "The standard way is a resistor divider from the output to the feedback pin of the controller. The IC has an internal reference, say 0.
6 volts, and an error amplifier that compares the feedback pin to that reference.
The loop adjusts the duty cycle until the feedback pin sits at exactly the reference, so the output ends up at V ref times (1 plus R 1 over R 2) , where R 1 is the top resistor and R 2 the bottom.
The divider is needed for two reasons. First, the reference is low, around 0. 6 to 1 volts, and the output is usually higher, so I have to scale it down to compare.
Second, it's how you program the output voltage with two resistors, rather than needing a custom IC for every rail. In a real design there's more around it.
There's usually a small feed-forward capacitor across the top resistor to add phase boost and speed up the loop.
The error amplifier has its own compensation network, either internal or external on a COMP pin.
And I'd connect the top of the divider at the load or right at the output capacitor with a Kelvin trace, away from the switch node, so it senses the real output and doesn't pick up noise."
